doc.title: Ralph Sutton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 22, 1995

title: Radio's Harlem Rhythm, Fats Waller and what to call the music
summary: He heard Ellington, Basie and Fats Waller on a St. Louis radio show; musicians did not label the music, laymen did.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: In Missouri, what kind of music did you hear as a child growing up?

Well there was a radio station in St. Louis, and they had a little program on there called “Harlem Rhythm,” a 15 minute program every morning. And that’s how I got started hearing Duke Ellington, Basie, and Fastolo Wolloro.

Well that’s Fats Waller. And I mentioned coming over today, Fats — Rochester was interviewing Fats one time and, “what is this thing, what kind of music you playing, Fats, this thing is swing or what?” Well Fats says, “You get that right tickin’ rhythm man and it’s on.”
Figure that out right? The right ticking rhythm.
Not, he didn’t put the “G” on it. The right tickin’ rhythm, man, it’s on.
You do that pretty well. You say that pretty well. When you were growing up and you were listening to that, was the music called, did it have a name? Was it called swing? Was it called jazz?

No, I think the laymen, the guys that couldn’t play anything and just listened, they had to put labels on things to understand what the guys were playing. But the musicians didn’t need to call it anything, you know.
I think it was the same thing when bop started. I think I read that the critics called it bop. The musicians just played it.
